cues.text: A Learned Noblewoman
According to her traditional Acts, Catherine was a young woman of noble birth in Alexandria , a city renowned across the ancient world.
It was a center of philosophy and learning, and she herself was said to be exceptionally educated in the sciences of her day.
At only eighteen, she presented herself before the persecuting emperor, named in the legend as Maximinus.
Other traditions call him Maxentius; she rebuked him openly for cruelty toward Christians and argued against pagan worship.
Defeating the Emperor's Philosophers
Astonished at the young woman's audacity and unable to match her learning himself, the emperor summoned a panel of the empire's finest scholars to debate and refute her.
According to the Catholic Encyclopedia, Catherine instead 'emerged from the debate victorious.'
Several philosophers sent to overturn her arguments were so moved by her eloquence that they declared themselves Christians on the spot—and were promptly put to death for it.
Converting the Empress
Furious, the emperor had Catherine scourged and imprisoned, but even this failed to contain her influence.
The empress herself, curious to meet so remarkable a prisoner, visited her cell with Porphyry, commander of the imperial troops.
Both, tradition holds, were so persuaded by Catherine's testimony that they too converted, were baptized, and were martyred soon after.
The Breaking Wheel
Undeterred by her continued success at winning converts even from prison, the emperor condemned Catherine to be torn apart on a spiked breaking wheel.
The device has ever since carried her name, the 'Catherine wheel.'
According to the legend, the instrument itself shattered miraculously the moment she touched it.
Its flying spikes killed several onlookers, and Catherine was finally put to death by beheading.
Legend of Mount Sinai
A later tradition, dating from around the eighth century, holds that angels carried Catherine's body to Mount Sinai .

Her remains were said to have been discovered around the year 800 by monks of the monastery Emperor Justinian had built there centuries earlier, originating the renowned Monastery of St. Catherine that still stands on the mountain today.
Legacy
Catherine became one of the most popular saints of the medieval West, numbered among the Fourteen Holy Helpers and credited by St. Joan of Arc as one of the heavenly voices that guided her mission.

Her reputation for learned, fearless argument in defense of the faith has made her, ever since, the patron of philosophers, students, and scholars — a role model for anyone called to defend Christian truth through reasoned conviction rather than force.
